title: Maximum flow: Edmonds-Karp vs Dinic
problem_statement: Given a directed network on vertices 0..n-1 with non-negative integer edge capacities (parallel and antiparallel edges allowed), a source s and a sink t != s, compute the value of a maximum s-t flow.

input.parameter: n = V = number of vertices; E denotes the number of edges.
input.size_measure: V + E edges with capacities (at most 100 in the harness), so arithmetic on capacities and flows is unit cost. Both bounds below are strongly polynomial (independent of the capacity values).

algorithms.name: Edmonds-Karp
algorithms.idea: Ford-Fulkerson with shortest augmenting paths: repeatedly find a fewest-edge s-t path in the residual graph by BFS and push its bottleneck capacity.
algorithms.pseudocode: while BFS finds an s-t path P in the residual graph: push min residual capacity along P
algorithms.time_complexity: O(V E^2) for E >= 1 (O(V) for E = 0): at most E (min(V - 1, E) + 1) <= V E augmentations, independent of the capacities (algorithm: Edmonds & Karp 1972), each costing O(V + E); O(V^5) on graphs without parallel edges (E <= V(V - 1)). Proved in PROOFS.md, section 3.
algorithms.correctness: PROOFS.md, sections 1-3: the residual arrays always hold a feasible flow of value `flow`; when breadth-first search no longer reaches t, the vertices reachable from s form a cut whose capacity equals the flow, so the flow is maximum (max-flow min-cut theorem, Ford & Fulkerson 1956). Termination: residual distances never decrease, and each arc is the bottleneck at most (min(V - 1, E) + 1)/2 times, which bounds the number of augmentations (algorithm: Edmonds & Karp 1972).

algorithms.name: Dinic (blocking flows)
algorithms.idea: Phases: build the BFS level graph of the residual network, then saturate it with a blocking flow found by depth-first searches with current-arc pointers. The s-t distance grows every phase.
algorithms.pseudocode: while t is reachable: levels = BFS(s); push a blocking flow along level-increasing edges (DFS with current-arc pointers)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(V^2 E) for E >= 1 (O(V) for E = 0): at most min(V - 1, E) phases with t reachable, plus the final breadth-first search, and O(V E) per blocking-flow phase; O(V^4) on graphs without parallel edges. Proved in PROOFS.md, section 4.
algorithms.correctness: PROOFS.md, section 4 (algorithm due to Dinic 1970). Within a phase an arc that is not admissible (positive residual capacity and level-increasing) never becomes admissible, and the current-arc pointers only pass arcs that are not admissible or lead to vertices with no admissible path to t; so each phase ends with a blocking flow, after which the s-t distance in the residual graph is strictly larger. When t is unreachable the flow is maximum by the max-flow min-cut theorem.

relationship: Upper bounds O(V E^2) -> O(V^2 E) (O(V^5) -> O(V^4) on graphs without parallel edges); the second upper bound is smaller whenever E = omega(V). The T3 tag is a classification by the published worst-case upper bounds of the two algorithms (background); PROOFS.md proves both bounds as upper bounds for these two implementations. No lower bound for Edmonds-Karp and no separation between the two algorithms is shown in this entry, so it does not show that Dinic is asymptotically faster. Edmonds-Karp runs one breadth-first search per augmenting path. Dinic augments along shortest paths until no path of the current shortest length remains, in one O(V E) blocking-flow phase. Both are worst-case upper bounds; the measured growth on random networks is far below both (see verification).

sources.title: Maximal flow through a network
Theoretical efficiency of the Edmonds-Karp algorithm for computing maximal flows
sources.note: Studies the theoretical efficiency of the Edmonds-Karp algorithm (per its title); the paper was not read for this entry, and nothing from it is used or implemented.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle on random digraphs (densities 0.15, 0.4, 1.0; capacities from [1, 100], [1, 3] or unit; with zero-capacity, parallel and antiparallel edges), layered networks and networks with t unreachable, n = 2..10, 12, 14 (oracle: minimum over all s-t cuts, by enumeration) and n = 30, 60 (oracle: only the bounds 0 <= flow <= min(capacity out of s, capacity into t)). Not raised to V2 (INCONCLUSIVE): no instance family attaining either worst-case bound was constructed. On the random dense networks of generate_scaling (G(n, 0.5), n = 20..160), experiments/2026-10-07_max_flow_probe.py measured alpha = 0.558 for Edmonds-Karp against V E^2 = Theta(n^5) and alpha = 0.479 for Dinic against V^2 E = Theta(n^4); both would fail. The counts explain why. Edmonds-Karp made 21, 40, 87, 176 augmentations for n = 20, 40, 80, 160 (about n, far below V E = 3820 ... 2040640), and Dinic needed only 4, 3, 2, 3 phases. Against lower powers the same timings gave alpha = 0.924 vs n^3 for Edmonds-Karp and 0.965 vs n^2 for Dinic. That is average-case growth on this family, not a test of the claimed bounds, so it is not recorded as a V2 claim. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves both implementations correct, the upper bounds O(V E^2) and O(V^2 E), the space bound, the flow-value bounds of the caveats and the matching reduction of the notes; tests/test_proofs_maxflow.py checks their computable parts (cut enumeration on 152 networks; breadth-first-search counts against the augmentation and phase bounds on the validator's sizes and on generate_scaling n = 20, 40, 80; tracemalloc peaks; 60 bipartite matchings).

caveats: Both time bounds are worst-case bounds that random networks do not approach; this entry does not demonstrate them empirically (V1). With integer capacities both implementations run in O((F + 1)(V + E)) time, where F is the maximum flow value: every augmentation raises the flow by at least 1, so there are at most F augmentations; every breadth-first search reads each adjacency list at most once; and every Dinic phase except the last augments at least once, so there are at most F + 1 phases, each costing O(V + E) plus O(V) per augmenting path. Since F <= C outdeg(s) for maximum capacity C (the cut around s), capacities <= 100 without parallel edges out of s give F <= 100 min(V - 1, E) and O((min(V, E) + 1)(V + E)) time, which is O(V E) for E >= 1 (PROOFS.md, section 6). So in that range, which includes generate_scaling, Dinic's O(V^2 E) is not attained along any sequence of networks with V -> infinity, and Edmonds-Karp's O(V E^2) along none with E -> infinity; on generate_scaling both run in O(n^3). Zadeh 1972 studies the efficiency of Edmonds-Karp (per its title; the paper was not read here); no worst-case construction is claimed or implemented in this entry. Other maximum-flow algorithms are catalogued in staging/max-flow-edmonds-karp-vs-almost-linear. On the random networks measured here Dinic was also faster in practice (6.0 ms vs 39 ms at n = 160 in one console run), but that is not evidence for the worst-case bounds.
notes: Maximum bipartite matching is the unit-capacity special case (source -> left side, the edges, right side -> sink, all capacities 1; proof in PROOFS.md, section 7; compare pairs/bipartite-matching-kuhn-vs-hopcroft-karp). The two algorithms here differ only in how much is done per BFS: one augmenting path (Edmonds-Karp) or a blocking flow (Dinic).
